articles.text: The range between Miles City and Glendive and as we are credibly informed, for a radius of fifty miles about Miles City and other parts of eastern Montana, clearly show the reason for the low price of cattle on the Chicago market. The range is absolutely bare in the places alluded to, owing to drought and grasshoppers. There is scarcely a ton of hay in sight all the way from Glendive to Miles, not enough in a place to even picket a horse. The Bad Lands stockmen can well congratulate themselves on having escaped both grasshoppers and drought and having hay to sell.
articles.summary: The range around Miles City and Glendive is bare from drought and grasshoppers, while Bad Lands stockmen escaped both and have hay to sell.

articles.text: A discovery has recently been made that, if verified, will be received with joy by residents of our county. The line dividing Dakota and Montana has recently been surveyed, the report sent in to Washington, and the official decision returned to the surveyor. If no mistake has been made, the boundary line, instead of running just the other side of Sentinel Butte, runs several miles the other side of Mingusville. There may be some mistake, however, but this will be decided soon. The people of Mingusville are as well pleased as our people will be over this change in boundary lines and it is certainly to be hoped that the survey will stand.
articles.summary: A new survey reportedly puts the Dakota–Montana line several miles beyond Mingusville rather than just past Sentinel Butte.

articles.text: The census enumeration of northern Dakota discloses the fact that of the fifty-eight counties enumerated, all but four have had their boundaries changed since 1880 and all but two of these since 1883. In some of these cases it was proper that the boundaries should be changed, but the history of four changes out of five is one of corruption and was the result of a deal in which personal gain and not public good was the end sought. The changes in the boundaries of Billings county for instance, although in spite of the schemers it is now a far better county than it was before, was the result of a deal, in which outside parties thought to derive a benefit. There has been but little, if any objection to our new boundaries, but that such a move could have been originated and carried to a successful issue without the consent and almost without the knowledge of the citizens of our county, is a very unfavorable comment on Dakota legislation.
articles.summary: Editorial on county-boundary changes in northern Dakota, calling the Billings county change the result of an outside deal.

articles.text: The census returns are all completed as far as concerns northern Dakota and have been forwarded to Washington. From the returns, it appears that Cass county heads the list with 21,085 inhabitants. Grand Forks comes next with 20,453, while Burleigh county is ninth with 5,354. There are fifty-eight counties enumerated in the northern Dakota census. Billings county stands twenty-eighth in the list as concerns inhabitants, we having 737. In material wealth, we are not lower than tenth. In the fifty-eight counties enumerated, there is a total of 152,199 inhabitants, 32,503 farms and 612 manufactories. The returns from southern Dakota have not yet been sent in, but the principal footings are as follows: inhabitants, 263,465; farms, 50,264; manufactories, 442. The totals for the Territory are as follows: inhabitants, 415,664; farms, 82,767, manufactories, 1,054. For the above figures, we are indebted to the Bismarck Tribune.
articles.summary: Northern Dakota census returns: Billings county ranks 28th with 737 inhabitants; Territory totals 415,664.

articles.text:
Figures are not always absolutely correct, but there is certainly a good deal of truth in the following figures. They were made by a couple of cowboys in answer to an inquiry as to how much
it would cost to take care of a herd of 5,000 steers for eighteen months:

Four work horses,............$400.00
Two sets harness,............60.00
One wagon,............95.00
One spring wagon,............125.00
Two men, 1 month,............80.00
Grub for two men,............20.00
1,000 feet lumber,............40.00
Tools,............25.00
Stoves,............50.00
Dishes, etc............30.00
10 men, 3 months,............1,200.00
4 men, 3 months,............2,400.00
6 men, 9 months,............2,160.00
1 cook, 18 months,............900.00
50 cow horses,............2,750.00
Provisions,............1,750.00
Extra men during beef time,..500.00
Total,............$12,585.00

The most profitable cattle to put in are two-year-olds at $20 each. These will net $30 when sold as three's. The net profit, according to the figures is then $50,000 in eighteen months on an original outlay of $100,000, exclusive of running expenses and loss. We would increase the running expenses at least $2.500 for incidentals and a manager. Five per cent. of loss would be about right, making $5,000. All the cattle could not be found at the end of eighteen months, but as four-year-olds, they would yield enough additional profit to pay all expenses of gathering. Our figures would then increase the total outlay to $20,085. This in turn, would be decreased by at least $2,500 from the sale of horses, wagons, etc., leaving a total outlay of $17,585, the net profit on the whole transaction being $32,415. The above figures may be modified somewhat, but good judges would be more apt to figure a larger profit than a less one on the deal.
articles.summary: Two cowboys' estimate of the cost and profit of running 5,000 steers for eighteen months.

articles.text: Our Chicago market report shows a lowering of prices all around, especially in grass-fed Texans and western range cattle, both dropping about fifty cents. Heavily increased arrivals of all classes of cattle was the cause of the depression. The arrivals of Texas and western cattle was 26,000 of which 17,000 were from Texas and about 4,000 from Dakota and Montana. Extra prime beeves were the only class to escape the general depression, they advancing ten to fifteen cents. The present outlook would seem to indicate that prices will be low for some time, as many cattle are now being sent to market that should stay on the range another year. There is also every chance that a large number will be marketed from the Indian Territory and this will result in another drop.
articles.summary: Chicago prices fell about fifty cents on grass-fed Texans and western range cattle due to heavy arrivals.

articles.headline: With the Cowboy.
articles.text:
It was late in the afternoon when we rode up the steep and rocky path that led into the green valley where round-up 34 was camped. On the rich hillsides the horses of the different outfits were being bunched up by the day herders, and the odor of fried bacon was being wafted from the camp-fire where Eli was officiating as cook. Sam. Basset had fed his hungry gang and was putting away the supper things, and in a little while the boys were rolling up their beds and seeking a shelter from the storm that was coming up. After everyone had finished his supper, the different camps put in order and the night herders sent out, all the rest of the boys gathered in the cabin to spend the evening. The two flickering candles stuck in empty beer bottles, shone over a motley looking crowd. There were twenty or twenty-five of them, ranging in age from the "kid" of fourteen to the old "broncho buster" of fifty. "Give us some music, cookey," called out one of the boys throwing a mouth organ to Fred. Reynolds. Clearing out his mouth and filling himself up with wind, Fred. blew the music out of the mouth organ with the skill of a born musician, and was greeted with great applause. Then an old fiddle belonging to a sleepy Dutchman was brought out and a grand quadrille improvised. It was an inspiring sight to see Watts promenade across the floor with Rocky Mountain Bob as a partner, jab his spur into the knee of a spectator and back Skinny Dick over a saddle. Probably John Cassius Templeton, the Colorado cowboy, was the most limber-legged of all the artists, and he would have attracted attention even in a Boston drawing room. "Jumbo" also waltzed with the tender grace of a young elephant, though the rest of the boys
had to climb up on the table and chairs to make room for his feet. The more intricate steps of the Newport and racquet were executed by that young but shining ornament of society, Charley Mellor.

A song from Lee was the unanimous demand when the fiddler was finally exhausted. "I can't sing," protested Walter with the modesty of true merit, but the excuse would not go down and he finally sang one song. A wild tempest of applause rose from the assembly at the conclusion of this song and there was scarcely a dry eye in the crowd as the last tender strain died away. A clog dance and a song by Fred the cook was the next demand, and was filled with neatness and dispatch. The dance was performed to the music of the harmonica in the agile mouth of the triple-tongued Englishman. The music was fine, the dance excellent, and the song that fluttered out doors, wandered up over the mountain and drove the coyotes back into their holes, was as follows:

I am cook of the cowboy's camp,
A dancing, roving, musical tramp.
I can fry a slice of bacon to the achme of perfection,
And my latest batch of duff will bear the closest of inspection.
I can boil a pot of 'taters 'till they are in the right condition,
And can handle the harmonica just like an old musician.
A break-down, clog or hornpipe I can dance with great agility,
And dish you out a plate of beans with even more facility.
I grind a mess of coffee every morning with dexterity,
And get the breakfast ready with unusual celerity.

"But no body will get up in time if you don't all go to bed pretty soon," broke in Charley Rader the foreman. The hint was sufficient. Beds were unrolled and spread out on the floor. The disrobing process was completed by taking off boots, spurs, coats and hats, and in a short time nothing was heard but the steady snore of the cowboys, the
whinney of a strayed horse, or the dismal howl of a lonesome coyote on the mountain.

Sunrise in the mountains! Can we find language to describe the scene that met our view after we had scrambled through the mountain cedars, and over the rocks to the top of the hill overlooking the camp. The rain of the night before had cleared the air, and earth and sky were resplendent with all the colors of sunrise. In the white cups of the mountain lillies hung the glistening tears into which the clouds had dissolved themselves, and a million raindrops were sparkling like diamonds from sage brush and cedar. A thin veil of mist rested lightly upon the rounded crest of the mountain across the valley. Far beyond—away to the southwest rose the Uinta mountains against the blue horizon; rugged, snow-crowned, and shining like polished marble in the morning sun. Nature is wide awake; the long eared jack-rabbit bounds lightly over the sage brush, the little birds call to each other from among the twisted cedars, and two old sage hens—looking as large as turkeys—come from behind a clump of grease wood.

In the camp below, the horses are being corralled; Jumbo is showing how many times he can throw his lasso at the white faced roan without catching her, and Albert the Kid, is untying himself from the fence where he has been fastened for safety. Isam Dart, the negro broncho buster, takes a tumble to himself as his horse stumbles into a badger hole, and George Scrivner is left to tackle the bucking bronchos that nobody else cares to handle. Soon we are all on the move; the 300 magnificent horses that are in the outfits are driven up the valley to the new camping place, the well mounted cowboys follow and the white covered wagons bring up the rear.—[Rock Springs (Wyo.) Independent.
articles.summary: Reprinted sketch from the Rock Springs (Wyo.) Independent of an evening and sunrise at a Wyoming round-up camp.

articles.headline: Joe Hampson's Proverbs.
articles.text:
Joe Hampson, one of the leading cattle men of southern New Mexico, has drifted into literature, and the following aphorisms are the latest efforts of his facile pen:

It's a cold day when you can freeze the horns off a Galloway bull.

A cow on the range is worth three steers in southern Texas.

It's a wise maverick that knows its own owner.

The green cowboy fears not the bucking broncho.

The road of the cowboy thief is the pen—if he's caught.

The wise cowboy brandeth calves daily for his master, while the foolish one bloweth in his substance in a jim-crow saloon.

It's a thoroughbred calf that knows its own sire.

Like unto the presence of teeth in the mouth of the female fowl, or the finding of double eagles in the pocket of an editor, so are fresh beef and milk on a well regulated cow ranch.

"[P]eople must read and eat beef, consequently newspapers and cattle ranches are two absolutely permanent institutions of this country."

[The following is a real old chestnut which we have cut out from the balance of the collection.—Ed.

The cowman who borrows money to live on at two per cent., who don't believe in improving his herd and who never reads the newspapers is like a cow's tail. (Joke.) [Answer: He's always behind.]
—[Numerous Exchanges.
articles.summary: Humorous cattleman's aphorisms attributed to New Mexico cattleman Joe Hampson, from exchanges.

articles.text: The Bad Lands cattle company will start on a beef round-up next Tuesday, beginning at Sentinel Butte, working Big and Little Beaver to their mouths, thence up the Little Missouri to the mouth of Garner. All wishing to join this round-up, will be at Sentinel Butte early Tuesday morning.

articles.text: It is rather a surprise party to learn that E. G. Paddock has been indicted for murder in connection with the Marquis, for the killing of Luffsey. There is certainly no evidence against him and the case must be dismissed for lack of evidence. The only reasonable explanation is that Mr. Paddock is one of the principal witnesses for the defense and the prosecution hope in this way to weaken his evidence.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock indicted for murder with the Marquis in the Luffsey killing; the Cow Boy calls it a prosecution tactic.

articles.text: The report was current here for some time and is still generally believed, that Half-breed Jack was hung for horse-stealing by vigilantes in Montana last summer. He is now in jail at Miles City, having been captured with Muley Bob. They both plead guilty to horse-stealing and were sentenced to a year each in the county jail. W[m.?] Roberas is in jail at the same place and professes perfect ignorance of the charge against him. It seems that he was first arrested on the charge of murder, but it has now been changed to that of horse-stealing.
articles.summary: Half-breed Jack and Muley Bob, captured together, sentenced to a year each for horse-stealing at Miles City.

articles.text: The cattle disease at Sentinel Butte is still unchecked. Only nine or ten head have died, but A. Osborne, who has a small bunch of cattle on Andrews creek states that the disease is contagious. In any event, something should be done immediately, as prevention is far better than cure in a case of this kind. We can scarcely explain the reason, but Fred. Willard, in writing for instructions as to how to act in this case, learned that there was no Dakota law in reference to contagious diseases. In this event, the work must be done by individual cowmen, and not by and by, but now.
articles.summary: Cattle disease at Sentinel Butte unchecked; no Dakota law on contagious diseases.

articles.text: MARRIED:—Wednesday, Aug. 26, at the Catholic church, in Medora, Dak., by the Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, Mary, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. M. M. Coleman, to John Goodall, both of Medora.
articles.summary: Marriage of Mary Coleman and John Goodall at the Catholic church, Medora, Aug. 26.

articles.text:
The above notice will be read with more interest and pleasure than that of
any we could publish in these columns. It is seldom that one can say as in this case, "They had no acquaintances. All were friends." The happy couple were well known in Medora and vicinity and we merely voice the sentiment of the entire community in wishing them a long life and every earthly enjoyment. The marriage at the church was followed by a reception and wedding lunch in the parlor of the Northern Pacific. The bride never looked prettier and the groom took a pardonable pride in the congratulations showered upon him. In the evening, Mr. and Mrs. Goodall joined with Mr. and Mrs. Munro, the bride and groom of a week ago, in giving a party at the Northern Pacific, in which all joined with the expectation of having a good time and none were disappointed. A bountiful supper was served at twelve o'clock. The dancing was kept up until about one, when the company dispersed, having registered in their minds another social success for Medora. Mr. and Mrs. Goodall were the recipients of several useful and valuable presents. An elegant walnut, marble-topped chamber set and full toilet set came from "the Gang," Marquise de Mores gave a handsome lamp, T. Martin presented some fine table cutlery and a silver butter-dish and castor-set were the gifts of Miss Alice Morrison and Martin Timlin. The bridal couple will board at the Northern Pacific for a time, at least.
articles.summary: Account of the Goodall wedding reception, evening party and gifts, including a lamp from the Marquise de Morès.

L. A. Huffman, Miles City's photographer, has "struck a new lead" that is and will be profitable. It is in the shape of a series of forty instantaneous photographic views of prominent stock ranches and the most interesting events of a round-up. The views were all taken from the saddle and are startlingly realistic in their illustrations of cowboy life. We are under many obligations to Mr. Huffman for a full set of these views and wish him abundant success in selling them. Single copies are twen-
ty-five cents; per dozen, two dollars; and the full set of forty for five dollars. They will be mailed to any address on receipt of price by L. A. Huffman, Miles City, Montana.

articles.text: The policy of patronizing home industries has lately received another argument in its favor in the matter of insurance rates. All rates are established by the companies, no choice being left to the agent. Among all companies, the rate charged on all classes of risks is nearly, if not exactly the same. The details differ somewhat in some companies accepting and others rejecting a class of risks, some will take a three-years risk at double the rate of a one-year risk while others will not, etc. In general, the charges are exactly alike. It will thus be seen that the local agent has every advantage over a visiting agent who must pay travelling and other expenses. An illustration of this arose recently where a travelling agent for an insurance company came here and quoted a $3 rate of $18 for insuring a risk of $600. The most that is asked by any company is a $1.75 rate or $10.50 for $600 insurance. To prove the matter conclusively, both rates were quoted by agents of the same company. The above is only an illustration of the broad principle, proved over and over again, that it is altogether better to patronize home industries wherever it is possible, thus increasing your neighbor's prosperity and consequently your own.
articles.summary: Editorial urging home insurance agents over travelling agents, citing an inflated quote.

articles.text:
As the Mandan Pioneer says, there will be much difficulty in finding an intelligent jury in this district, none of whom have expressed an opinion in the case of the Territory vs. Marquis de Mores, for murder. In other states and territories a person indicted for this offense is not allowed to furnish bail, but the law passed at the last session of the legislature makes the offense bailable. The Marquis started west from New York yesterday and will probably be in Mandan in a day or two. We have already expressed our opinion and that of the
entire community in reference to bringing up this case again. Everyone wanted the matter to drop, except a few blood-sucking lawyers. The whole matter was adjusted as well as could be and the additional expense of the trial is entirely unwarranted. Eastern papers have been publishing such highly colored accounts of the affair, that for the benefit of those of our readers living there, it may be best to publish an outline of the case. In the summer and fall of 1883, a few months after the Marquis came here, he began fencing some land he had bought. Before he had finished the fencing, several persons expressed decided opinions concerning it, unless gates were left in the places where the roads ran. From this arose Frank O'Donald's remark about shooting the Marquis on sight. That he was drunk when he made it, no one who knows him can doubt. When drunk, he recognizes neither friend nor enemy, but wants to pick a quarrel with everyone. When sober, he is as peaceable as he is quarrelsome when drunk. O'Donald's remark was carried to the Marquis, who considering his life in danger, telegraphed to Mandan for officers. O'Donald was in Little Missouri when the sheriff arrived. He was drunk and defied the officer. Riding out of town with Luffsey and Wonegan, the Marquis and party were met and Luffsey was killed. Eastern papers have been fond of referring to Luffsey and Wonegan as desperadoes when the fact is they were quiet, peaceable hunters, who only happened to be with O'Donald and whose innocence there was, of course, no time to establish when the shooting began. The whole affair arose in misunderstanding [the?] true sentiment on both sides. Wonegan is now in Mandan to release his bondsmen in the present case, while O'Donald has left the country. As we said before, no one here wanted the case brought up again, it is a useless expense to the county and will serve no purpose except as a benefit to the lawyers employed.
articles.summary: Editorial on the renewed murder case against the Marquis de Morès, with the paper's outline of the 1883 Luffsey shooting.
